source_text: Cum ergo hoc tam magnum apertum esset, quid illud fuit, quod tibi persuasit, ut crederes antiqui nihili violentiam causam malae voluntatis fuisse? Profecto ut intellegeremus nos, omnia te, quae sunt facta de nihilo, rea credere, et universum mundum diabolo mancipare. Quoniam igitur mihi claruit antiquam inter vos dogmatum manere concordiam, hinc iam tibi pariter et Manichaeo respondeo. Quaeritis certe, ut qui nego mali esse naturam, si possum respondeam, unde ipsa mala voluntas in homine primo potuit exoriri. At ego refero non vos intellegere quid dicatis. Voluntas enim nihil est aliud, quam motus animi, cogente nullo.
pass_a_gloss: When therefore this so great thing was open, what was that which persuaded you to believe that the violence of the ancient nothing was the cause of an evil will? Surely that we might understand that you believe all things which were made from nothing guilty, and enslave the whole world to the devil. Since therefore it became clear to me that an ancient concord of dogmas remains between you, from here now I reply equally to you and to Manichaeus. You ask certainly, that I who deny that there is a nature of evil, if I can, reply from where the evil will itself could arise in the first human. But I report that you do not understand what you say. For will is nothing other than a motion of the mind, no one compelling.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: Since this great point was so plain, what persuaded you to believe that the violence of ancient nothing was the cause of an evil will? Certainly it was so that we could understand that you believe everything made from nothing guilty and enslave the whole world to the devil. Since it has become clear to me that your ancient doctrinal agreement remains, I now answer you and Mani together. You ask me, who deny that evil has a nature, to answer if I can: where could the evil will itself arise in the first human being? I reply that you do not understand what you are saying. For will is nothing other than a movement of the mind under no compulsion.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
